#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Add ONE entry to the dataset.

Usage: echo '{"prompt": "...", "response": "..."}' | python3 scripts/add_entry.py
"""
import hashlib, json, os, sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
DATA = os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "entries.dat")
DIGEST = os.path.join(ROOT, "data", ".digest")


def file_digest(path):
    return hashlib.sha256(open(path, "rb").read()).hexdigest()


def main():
    raw = sys.argv[1]
    try:
        entry = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        sys.exit("E11: could not parse entry: %s" % e)
    if not isinstance(entry, dict) or sorted(entry) != ["prompt", "response"]:
        sys.exit('E12: entry must be a JSON object with exactly the keys "prompt" and "response"')
    if not all(isinstance(entry[k], str) and entry[k].strip() for k in entry):
        sys.exit("E13: prompt and response must be non-empty strings")
    if os.path.exists(DIGEST) and file_digest(DATA) != open(DIGEST).read().strip():
        sys.exit("E17: dataset integrity check failed; refusing to append")
    with open(DATA, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    with open(DIGEST, "w") as f:
        f.write(file_digest(DATA))
    print("OK: entry added")


main()
</tool_response>

final_entries.prompt: I moved to a new city for work and I miss everyone from home. I don't know anyone here yet.
final_entries.response: Moving to a new city is one of those transitions that looks clean on paper but feels incredibly lonely in practice. It's completely normal to miss the easy connections you've built with people who know your history. You're not failing at this — you're just in that in-between phase where the old comfort is gone and the new ones haven't taken root yet. One small step at a time helps: a coffee shop you can become regular at, a class where you see the same faces, or even just saying hi to the same person at the grocery store. The first genuine friend in a new city often starts as just the person you nod at every Thursday morning. This phase will pass, and in the meantime, it's okay to grieve what feels far away.

final_entries.prompt: I have a panic attack coming up at the dentist appointment next week and I'm terrified.
final_entries.response: That fear is so valid — dental anxiety is one of the most common fears people have, and you are not alone or weak for feeling this way. First, know that your feelings matter and you get to advocate for yourself. When you call the office, you can tell them you have dental anxiety. Many dentists are used to working with nervous patients and can take extra steps: letting you bring headphones, giving you a signal to pause whenever you need it, or even offering something to help you relax. You might also practice some breathing exercises in the days leading up to your appointment — just slow, deep breaths that remind your body it's safe. Whatever you choose, remember that asking for support isn't a weakness; it's a sign that you care about your wellbeing enough to face something difficult.

final_entries.prompt: I'm trying to learn to cook but everything I make tastes terrible. Maybe I should just give up.
final_entries.response: Oh, please don't give up — you're exactly where every single cook was when they started, even the ones who now make incredible food. The gap between what you're making now and what you want to make is not a measure of your ability; it's just a distance you need to walk across, one slightly-better dish at a time. A few gentle suggestions if you want them: start with recipes that have five ingredients or fewer, taste as you go rather than waiting until the end, and don't beat yourself up when things go wrong — that slightly-burnt garlic is basically a badge of honor at this stage. You're building a skill that will serve you for the rest of your life, and the fact that you're even trying shows real determination. Be patient with yourself; the food will get better.

final_entries.prompt: My teenage daughter barely talks to me anymore and it's really lonely being a parent sometimes.
final_entries.response: What you're feeling is deeply real and it takes courage to name it out loud. Parenting an adolescent can feel like watching someone you love deeply slowly build a door between you, and it's painful to stand on the other side of it. But please hear this: their pulling away is almost certainly not about you personally — it's their brain and body going through an enormous restructuring, and part of what teenagers do is push away the very people who love them most as they figure out who they are outside your shadow. The love is still there, even when the door is closed. You can keep leaving it slightly ajar: a snack left on their desk, a text with no expectation of reply, a song you think they'd like. Sometimes the best thing you can do is just stay steady and present while they sort themselves out. And it's okay — more than okay — to find other parents in the same boat so you don't have to carry this loneliness alone.

final_entries.prompt: I keep comparing myself to my coworkers who seem to have it all together and it's making me miserable.
final_entries.response: Comparison is such a cruel thief of peace, isn't it? The tricky part is that you're comparing your behind-the-scenes — with all its doubts, messy drafts, and private uncertainties — to everyone else's highlight reel. What you see are the polished presentations, the confident emails, the smooth meetings. What you don't see are the hours of preparation, the imposter syndrome they're hiding, the mistakes they don't advertise. You're not falling behind; you're on your own path, which has its own timing and milestones that nobody else gets to judge. Instead of asking 'why don't I measure up to them?' try asking 'what does today's version of good look like for me?' Celebrate the small wins — the email you finally sent, the meeting you showed up to even though you felt unprepared. You are enough exactly as you are in this season.

final_entries.prompt: I'm 42 and still don't have a career figured out. Everyone else seems to have their life together.
final_entries.response: Forty-two is not too late — it's honestly the perfect age to start figuring things out, because you finally have enough life experience to know what doesn't work for you. And for the record, a lot of the people who seem to have it all together are just better at looking busy. Career paths have rarely been straight lines, even for the people who make them look effortless. What matters right now is not catching up to an imaginary timeline but getting curious about what genuinely interests you. What tasks make you lose track of time? What problems do you enjoy solving? You don't need a five-year plan; you need one small step that feels meaningful. Maybe it's an informational interview with someone in a field you're curious about, maybe it's a free online course, maybe it's just journaling about what you'd do if money weren't a concern. Whatever you choose, give yourself permission to be a beginner again. Your past isn't wasted — it's preparation, even if it doesn't look like it yet.
